{{Short description|Measure of an object's size along a specified direction}}
[[File:Feret diameter.png|thumb|Illustration of horizontal and vertical Feret diameters of a particle, Fh and Fv, respectively.]]
[[File:DigitalCaliperEuro.jpg|thumb|The diameter of an object measured with a [[caliper]] is sometimes called the caliper diameter; it is the same as Feret diameter.]]
[[File:Diamètre de feret.jpg|thumb|Feret diameter applied to a projection of a 3D object.]]

The '''Feret diameter''' or '''Feret's diameter''' is a measure of an object's size along a specified direction. In general, it can be defined as the distance between the two parallel planes restricting the object perpendicular to that direction. It is therefore also called the '''caliper diameter''', referring to the measurement of the object size with a [[caliper]]. This measure is used in the analysis of [[Particle size (grain size)|particle sizes]], for example in [[microscopy]], where it is applied to [[3D projection|projections]] of a three-dimensional (3D) object on a 2D plane. In such cases, the Feret diameter is defined as the distance between two parallel tangential ''lines'' rather than ''planes''.<ref name=r1/><ref name=r2/>

==Mathematical properties==
From [[Cauchy's theorem (geometry)|Cauchy's theorem]] it follows that for a 2D [[convex body]], the Feret diameter averaged over all directions (〈F〉) is equal to the ratio of the object [[perimeter]] (P) and [[pi]], i.e.,〈F〉=  P/{{pi}}. There is no such relation between〈F〉and P for a [[wikt:concave|concave]] object.<ref name=r1/><ref name=r2/>

==Applications==
Feret diameter is used in the analysis of particle size and its distribution, e.g. in a powder or a polycrystalline solid; alternative measures include [[Martin diameter]], [[Krumbein diameter]] and [[Heywood diameter]].<ref name=r3/> The term first became common in scientific literature in the 1970s<ref name=r4/> and can be traced to L.R. Feret (after whom the diameter is named) in the 1930s. <ref name=r5/>

It is also used in biology as a method to analyze the size of cells in tissue sections.
